text: 1.e4 brings a pawn to the centre: it occupies e4 and controls d5 and f5.
It also opens two lines: those of the bishop on f1 and the queen on d1, which can come out at once.
1.d4 occupies the centre with the queen's pawn: it controls c5 and e5.
The pawn on d4 is defended by the queen on d1, and the diagonal of the bishop on c1 opens.
After 1.e4 e5, 2.Nf3 develops a piece and at the same time attacks the pawn on e5.
Black usually answers by defending e5 (with the knight, the d-pawn or the f-pawn) or by attacking the pawn on e4 in turn.
With 1...c5 Black does not put a pawn on e5: it controls d4 with a side pawn.
If White pushes d4, Black's c-pawn is often exchanged for White's d-pawn: the c-file opens for Black and White keeps one more central pawn.
1...d5 immediately attacks the pawn on e4.
After 2.exd5 Black often recaptures with the queen, which can however be attacked by the developing white pieces (for example a knight on c3).
1...e6 prepares 2...d5, which attacks the pawn on e4 with the support of the pawn on e6.
The bishop on c8 stays shut in behind the black pawns on e6 and d5: freeing it is a typical theme of Black's game.
1...c6 prepares 2...d5, which attacks the pawn on e4 with the pawn on c6 as support.
Unlike the French, the diagonal of the bishop on c8 stays open: the bishop often comes out before the e-pawn is pushed.
1...Nf6 develops a piece and controls e4 and d5 without putting a pawn in the centre right away.
Many openings with different names start from here (King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Grünfeld…), depending on where Black develops the bishop and when the central pawns are pushed.
3.Bc4 develops the bishop on a diagonal aimed at f7, the square next to the black king defended only by the king.
After 3.Bc4 White has cleared the squares between king and rook: castling short is possible on the next move.
2.c4 offers the c-pawn to attack the black pawn on d5 and fight for the centre.
Black can take it (Queen's Gambit Accepted) or defend d5 with a pawn, for example with e6 or c6 (Queen's Gambit Declined, Slav).
1.Nf3 develops a knight that controls e5 and d4 without deciding yet which central pawn to push.
With the following moves it can lead to many different openings: it is one of the first moves that most often lead to transpositions.
2.Bc4 develops the bishop at once on the diagonal aimed at f7.
The knight on g1 stays home for now: White can still choose between Nf3 and the push f4.
1.c4 controls d5 with a side pawn instead of occupying the centre with e4 or d4.
White often develops the bishop on g2 (after g3), where it looks along the long diagonal towards the centre and the queenside.
2...d6 defends the pawn on e5 with a pawn instead of a piece.
The diagonal of the bishop on f8 stays closed by the pawn on d6: the bishop is usually developed to e7.
1...e6 opens the diagonal of the bishop on f8 and prepares d5 or f5.
It can transpose into other openings: for example a French, if White plays e4 and Black answers d5.
3.Bb5 attacks the knight on c6, the piece that defends the pawn on e5.
Black often asks the bishop at once with a6: the bishop can retreat to a4 or exchange itself for the knight.
3.d4 immediately attacks the pawn on e5 with a pawn and opens the centre.
After 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 the white knight stands in the centre on d4 and White has the pawn on e4 against no black central pawn.
2.Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
The f3 square stays free for the f-pawn: the push f4 against the pawn on e5 is one of the themes of the Vienna.
2.d4 immediately attacks the pawn on e5 with the queen's pawn.
If Black captures and White recaptures with the queen (3.Qxd4), the queen stands in the centre but can be attacked by a knight coming out to c6.
1...e5 offers the e-pawn: after 2.dxe5 the white pawn arrives on e5.
In return for the pawn Black aims for quick development of the pieces and attacks on the pawn on e5.
